title: Trump Administration Floats Subsidizing Parents To Raise Children At Home
text:
(Photo by OLIVIER TOURON/AFP via Getty Images)

The Trump administration wants to pay married parents to stay home and raise their own kids.

Officials are drafting a rule that would let married couples with one stay-at-home spouse tap federal child care subsidies, a priority of Vice President JD Vance, the New York Times reported. The plan would carve out a new category the draft calls “parent-based child care,” letting one married parent draw assistance to care for their child while the other works at least 35 hours a week, according to the Times.

The change could take effect as soon as next year and would not need a vote in Congress, though it requires White House approval and a public comment window. (RELATED: EXCLUSIVE: GOP Senators Target Rampant Child Care Fraud In New Bill)

The money would come from the Child Care and Development Fund, a roughly $12 billion program administered by the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). Congress created the fund under the 1990 Child Care and Development Block Grant Act to help low-income families afford care so parents could work or attend school, according to the Congressional Research Service. States distribute the aid through vouchers or direct payments to providers, and it averages about $9,000 per child each year, according to the Times.

Breaking News: A Trump administration plan would direct child-care funds to married stay-at-home parents, people familiar with the plan say. https://t.co/BuG178XKbb

Redirecting that pot toward at-home parents worries critics who say the fund cannot stretch further without new dollars. Roughly 80% of the 870,000 families now collecting the subsidy are headed by single working parents, most of them mothers, according to Health Department figures cited by the Times.

“Expanding the eligibility without increasing funding would mean more parents competing for the same dollars, and leaving more parents — particularly single working parents — worse off,” Joshua McCabe of the Niskanen Center told the Times.

The draft limits the benefit to married couples, leaving out unmarried couples and single parents who do not work, according to the Times. Some department attorneys have questioned whether tying eligibility to marriage can survive a legal challenge and warned the shift could invite fraud.

Vance advocated for a similar policy when he was in the senate. In a September 2024 post on X, he argued that federal and state policy penalizes in-home and kinship care by subsidizing a single model of child care. The draft also borrows from legislation Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote as a senator.

Roger Severino of the Heritage Foundation, who authored the Project 2025 section on child care, defended the approach. “It would be a welcome change to see equal treatment between commercial day care and the contribution stay-at-home parents provide in caring for and raising the next generation,” he told the Times.
